cache.invalidate.name: cache.invalidate
cache.invalidate.summary: Removes an instance from the reference cache.
cache.invalidate.purpose: Removes an instance from the engine's reference cache. The next time the game looks that instance up, it gets a fresh object, and any reference it stored earlier no longer matches — which is how you make a specific object stop being tracked.
cache.invalidate.example:
cache.invalidate(workspace.Part)
print(workspace.Part == oldReference)   -- false, the cache entry is gone
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Aggressive use destabilises the game's own references. Invalidate the one object you mean to.

cache.iscached.summary: Returns whether or not an instance exists within the reference cache.
cache.iscached.purpose: Checks whether an instance is currently in the reference cache, which tells you whether an earlier invalidate took effect.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

cache.replace.name: cache.replace
cache.replace.summary: Replaces an instance with another instance in the internal instance cache.
cache.replace.purpose: Swaps the object the cache returns for a given instance, so every future lookup of that instance hands back something else. Where cloneref changes your reference, this changes the game's.
cache.replace.example:

print(workspace.Part)   -- resolves to OtherPart
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Type mismatches between the two instances cause errors in game code that expected the original.

checkcaller.name: checkcaller
checkcaller.summary: Returns whether the current function was invoked from the executor's own thread rather than by the game.
checkcaller.purpose: Inside a hook you are running on whichever thread made the call, which could be the game or could be you. checkcaller answers which one, so a hook can pass your own calls straight through and only interfere with the game's. Without it, every hook you write eventually intercepts itself.
checkcaller.example:
local oldIndex
oldIndex = hookmetamethod(game, "__index", function(self, key)
    if checkcaller() then
        -- our own code, don't interfere
        return oldIndex(self, key)
    end
    if key == "Health" then
        return 100
    end
    return oldIndex(self, key)
end)
gotchas: Returns true inside your own thread even deep in nested calls, which is what you want.
It answers about the running thread, not the calling script. For that, use getcallingscript.

clonefunction.name: clonefunction
clonefunction.summary: Creates and returns a new function with the exact same behaviour as the passed function.
clonefunction.purpose: Gives you a separate function object with identical behaviour. Because it is a different object, hooking or comparing one does not affect the other, which makes it the standard way to stash a private copy of a function before the game or another script tampers with it.
clonefunction.example:
local safePrint = clonefunction(print)
-- Even if something hooks `print` later, safePrint still prints
hookfunction(print, function() end)
safePrint("still visible")
gotchas: The clone is not equal (==) to the original, which is the point, but it means identity checks against the original fail.

cloneref.name: cloneref
cloneref.summary: Returns a reference clone of an Instance. The returned object behaves identically but is not strictly equal (==) to the original.
cloneref.purpose: Games detect tampering by comparing instance references: if the LocalPlayer object you hold is the same object the game holds, anything you do to it is attributable. cloneref returns a second reference to the same underlying instance that is not equal (==) to the original, so your access does not show up in identity checks.
cloneref.example:
local player = cloneref(game:GetService("Players").LocalPlayer)
print(player == game.Players.LocalPlayer)   -- false
print(player.Name)                          -- but it is the same player
gotchas: Because == fails, any game code comparing your reference to theirs behaves differently. Use compareinstances to test equality yourself.
Cloning does not hide property changes; it hides reference identity only.

compareinstances.name: compareinstances
compareinstances.signature: function compareinstances(object1: Instance, object2: Instance): boolean
compareinstances.summary: Checks if two Instances are equal, even when one or both are reference clones.
compareinstances.purpose: Once cloneref is in play, == stops being a reliable way to ask 'are these the same object'. compareinstances answers that question properly by comparing the underlying instances rather than the references.
compareinstances.example:
local a = game:GetService("Players").LocalPlayer
local b = cloneref(a)
print(a == b)                    -- false
print(compareinstances(a, b))    -- true

debug.getcallstack.summary: Returns a table of the entire stack's information: source, line, what, name and func.
debug.getcallstack.purpose: Returns the whole call chain at once — every level's source, line, type and function — instead of walking levels one at a time. Inside a hook it answers the question a __namecall hook cannot: who actually called this.
debug.getcallstack.example:
for level, frame in ipairs(debug.getcallstack()) do
    print(level, frame.source, frame.line, frame.what)
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Includes your own frames unless you filter them out.

debug.getconstant.name: debug.getconstant
debug.getconstant.signature: function debug.getconstant(func: (...any) -> (...any) | number, index: number): number | string | boolean | nil
debug.getconstant.summary: Returns the constant at the specified index from a Luau function, or nil if none exists there.
debug.getconstant.purpose: Reads one constant by index instead of pulling the whole table. Useful in a loop that checks a known slot, or when you already know where the value you care about sits.
debug.getconstant.example:
local value = debug.getconstant(target, 1)
print(value)  -- the first constant in the function
gotchas: Returns nil for an index with no constant rather than erroring.

debug.getconstants.name: debug.getconstants
debug.getconstants.signature: function debug.getconstants(func: (...any) -> (...any) | number): { number | string | boolean | nil }
debug.getconstants.summary: Returns a list of all constants used within a Luau function's bytecode.
debug.getconstants.purpose: When Luau compiles a function, every literal in it — numbers, strings, the names of globals it calls — is stored in a constant table attached to the bytecode. Reading that table tells you what a function references without having its source, which is how you identify the right function among hundreds of similar ones.
debug.getconstants.example:
local function target()
    local speed = 16
    return game:GetService("Players")
end

for i, constant in ipairs(debug.getconstants(target)) do
    print(i, constant)   -- 16, "game", "GetService", "Players"
end
gotchas: C closures have no constants. Check islclosure first or you will error.
Indices are not stable across game updates; match on values, not positions.
You can pass a stack level (a number) instead of a function.

debug.getinfo.name: debug.getinfo
debug.getinfo.summary: Returns a table of information derived from a function or stack level.
debug.getinfo.purpose: The general-purpose introspection call: source, defining line, closure type, name, upvalue count and the function itself. It is the first thing to reach for when you have a function and no idea what it is.
debug.getinfo.example:
local info = debug.getinfo(someFunction)
print(info.source, info.linedefined, info.what, info.nups)
gotchas: Field availability differs slightly between executors; guard reads on optional fields.
Accepts a stack level as well as a function.

debug.getproto.name: debug.getproto
debug.getproto.signature: function debug.getproto(func: (...any) -> (...any) | number, index: number, activated: boolean?): (...any) -> (...any) | { (...any) -> (...any) }
debug.getproto.summary: Returns a specific function prototype by index. With activated set to true it returns currently active closures made from that proto.
debug.getproto.purpose: Fetches one nested prototype by index, and optionally the live closures created from it. The second form is the important one: it gives you the actual running instances of an inner function, with their real upvalues attached.
debug.getproto.example:
-- The template (upvalues empty)
local template = debug.getproto(outer, 1)

-- Every live closure made from that template
local active = debug.getproto(outer, 1, true)
for _, fn in ipairs(active) do
    print(debug.getupvalues(fn))  -- real captured state
end
gotchas: Without activated = true you get a clone with no state, and calling it usually errors on a nil upvalue.
The activated form scans the GC and is comparatively slow.

debug.getprotos.name: debug.getprotos
debug.getprotos.summary: Returns all function prototypes defined within the specified Luau function.
debug.getprotos.purpose: A proto is the compiled template of a function defined inside another function. Listing them lets you reach nested functions that were never assigned to a variable you can see — anonymous callbacks, inner helpers, connection handlers defined inline.
debug.getprotos.example:
local function outer()
    local function inner() return "hidden" end
    return inner
end

for i, proto in ipairs(debug.getprotos(outer)) do
    print(i, proto)   -- the inner function's prototype
end
gotchas: A proto is a template, not a live closure. Its upvalues are empty until you request active instances via debug.getproto with activated set to true.

debug.getregistry.name: debug.getregistry
debug.getregistry.summary: Returns the global registry table, which holds strong references that are never collected.
debug.getregistry.purpose: Potassium's name for the Luau registry table, the same structure getreg returns. Objects referenced here are never collected, which makes it a reliable place to find long-lived engine callbacks and threads.
debug.getregistry.example:
for key, value in pairs(debug.getregistry()) do
    if typeof(value) == "Instance" then print(key, value) end
end
gotchas: Writing here creates a permanent reference and leaks memory.

debug.getsafeenv.name: debug.getsafeenv
debug.getsafeenv.purpose: safeenv is a Luau optimisation flag: when it is set, the VM assumes a thread's global table has not been tampered with and takes fast paths that ignore metatable hooks on globals. Reading the flag tells you whether those hooks would be respected.
debug.getsafeenv.example: print(debug.getsafeenv())  -- true means globals are on the fast path
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
If safeenv is on, hooks on the global table can appear to do nothing.

debug.getstack.name: debug.getstack
debug.getstack.signature: function debug.getstack(level: number, index: number?): any | { any }
debug.getstack.summary: Retrieves values from the stack at the specified call level.
debug.getstack.purpose: Exposes the values sitting in a stack frame while it runs — arguments, locals, temporaries. Inside a hook this lets you read what the caller is working with even when none of it was passed to you.
debug.getstack.example:
local function inspect()
    -- level 1 is this function, level 2 is our caller
    for i, value in ipairs(debug.getstack(2)) do
        print(i, value)
    end
end
gotchas: Levels shift as the call chain changes. A level that is correct in one hook is wrong in another.
Reading past the end of a frame errors on some implementations and returns nil on others.

debug.getupvalue.name: debug.getupvalue
debug.getupvalue.signature: function debug.getupvalue(func: (...any) -> (...any) | number, index: number): any
debug.getupvalue.summary: Returns the upvalue at the specified index from a function's closure. Errors if the index is out of bounds.
debug.getupvalue.purpose: Reads a single captured variable by index, for when you already know which slot holds the state you want.
gotchas: Errors on an out-of-range index, unlike debug.getconstant which returns nil.

debug.getupvalues.name: debug.getupvalues
debug.getupvalues.summary: Returns a list of upvalues captured by a Luau function.
debug.getupvalues.purpose: Upvalues are the variables a closure captured from the scope around it — the local state a function carries with it. Reading them is how you inspect a running system's private data when the only handle you have is one of its functions.
debug.getupvalues.example:
local counter = 0
local function increment()
    counter = counter + 1   -- `counter` is an upvalue
end

for i, upvalue in pairs(debug.getupvalues(increment)) do
    print(i, upvalue)       -- 1, 0
end
gotchas: Only Lua closures have upvalues.
The returned table is a snapshot of values, not live references; changing it does nothing.

debug.isvalidlevel.name: debug.isvalidlevel
debug.isvalidlevel.summary: Checks if a level is valid in the stack.
debug.isvalidlevel.purpose: Checks that a stack level exists before you read from it, so stack walking can stop cleanly instead of erroring at the top of the chain.
debug.isvalidlevel.example:
local level = 1
while debug.isvalidlevel(level) do
    print(level, debug.getinfo(level).source)
    level += 1
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

debug.setconstant.name: debug.setconstant
debug.setconstant.signature: function debug.setconstant(func: (...any) -> (...any) | number, index: number, value: number | string | boolean | nil): ()
debug.setconstant.summary: Modifies a constant at the specified index in a Luau function's bytecode.
debug.setconstant.purpose: Rewrites a literal inside a compiled function. This is patching without hooking: the function keeps its identity, its address and its hash-relevant structure mostly intact, but the number or string it uses is now yours.
debug.setconstant.example:
local function getDamage()
    return 10
end

debug.setconstant(getDamage, 1, 999)  -- swap the literal 10 for 999
print(getDamage())                    -- 999
gotchas: The new value must be the same kind of constant. Replacing a number with a table does not work.
Changes every call site of that function, since you edited the function itself.
Editing a constant changes the function's hash, so hash-based integrity checks will notice.

debug.setinfo.name: debug.setinfo
debug.setinfo.summary: Sets the debug info around a function.
debug.setinfo.purpose: Rewrites the metadata a function reports about itself, such as its source name or defined line. Used to make an executor-created function present the same identifying details as a game function.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Changes reporting only; the bytecode is untouched.

debug.setname.name: debug.setname
debug.setname.summary: Changes the function name to the set one.
debug.setname.purpose: Sets the name a function reports, which is what appears in stack traces and error messages. Mostly useful for making your own tooling readable, and for matching a game function's naming when a hook would otherwise stand out.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

debug.setsafeenv.name: debug.setsafeenv
debug.setsafeenv.summary: Marks the safeenv for an object.
debug.setsafeenv.purpose: Turns the safeenv optimisation off for an environment so that metatable hooks on globals actually fire. This is the fix for the common confusion where a __index hook on the global table appears to be ignored.
debug.setsafeenv.example: debug.setsafeenv(getrenv(), false)  -- make global hooks take effect
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Disabling it slows global access for the whole environment and is detectable.

debug.setstack.name: debug.setstack
debug.setstack.signature: function debug.setstack(level: number, index: number, value: any): ()
debug.setstack.summary: Replaces a value in a specified stack frame.
debug.setstack.purpose: Writes a value into a live stack frame, changing what the currently-executing function is holding. It is the most surgical patch available: no hook, no function replacement, just a different value in a register mid-call.
debug.setstack.example:
-- Inside a hook, replace the caller's first stack slot
debug.setstack(2, 1, 9999)
gotchas: Type must match what the frame expects, or you crash the thread rather than getting an error.
Extremely position-dependent; the smallest game update changes register allocation.

debug.setupvalue.name: debug.setupvalue
debug.setupvalue.signature: function debug.setupvalue(func: (...any) -> (...any) | number, index: number, value: any): ()
debug.setupvalue.summary: Replaces an upvalue at the specified index in a Luau function with a new value.
debug.setupvalue.purpose: Writes to a closure's captured state. Where setconstant edits a literal baked into the code, setupvalue edits live state the function is using, which makes it the right tool when the value changes at runtime.
gotchas: Other closures sharing the same upvalue see the change too, because they share the same cell.
Type-mismatched writes are accepted and will error later, at the point of use.

decompile.name: decompile
decompile.summary: Attempts to reconstruct readable Luau source from a script's bytecode.
decompile.purpose: Attempts to reconstruct readable Luau source from a script's bytecode. Output is never the original file — variable names are gone and control flow is rebuilt — but it is usually enough to understand what a script does.
gotchas: Potassium-specific; not part of the sUNC standard.
Output quality varies. Complex control flow and heavy optimisation produce source that will not recompile.
Slow on large scripts. Do not call it in a loop.

delfile.name: delfile
delfile.summary: Deletes the file at the specified path if it exists.
delfile.purpose: Deletes a single file. Used for cache invalidation and for cleaning up after a script that stored temporary data.
gotchas: Errors on a missing path in some implementations. Guard with isfile.

delfolder.name: delfolder
delfolder.summary: Deletes the folder at the specified path if it exists.
delfolder.purpose: Deletes a directory and what it contains. The heavy version of delfile, for removing an entire script's stored state at once.
gotchas: Recursive and irreversible. There is no recycle bin here.

dofile.name: dofile
dofile.summary: Attempts to execute the contents of a file.
dofile.purpose: Compiles and immediately runs a file, the one-step version of loadfile. Convenient for loading a script you saved locally.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Errors inside the file propagate to your script. Wrap in pcall if you want to survive them.

dumpbytecode.name: dumpbytecode
dumpbytecode.summary: Dumps a function into the Luau bytecode format. The target cannot be a C function.
dumpbytecode.purpose: Serialises a function back into Luau bytecode format, which is the reverse of loading a function and the input format for external analysis tools.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
C functions have no bytecode and will fail.

filtergc.name: filtergc
filtergc.signature: function filtergc(filterType: "function" | "table", filterOptions: table, returnOne: boolean?): any
filtergc.summary: Retrieves specific garbage-collected values from Luau's memory using fine-tuned filters.
filtergc.purpose: getgc with the search built in. Instead of scanning every object yourself, you describe what you are looking for — a function with a given name and upvalue, a table with certain keys — and the executor does the matching natively, which is far faster and far less code.
gotchas: Filter option names are case-sensitive and differ slightly between executors. Check the reference before assuming.
returnOne changes the return type from a table of matches to a single value or nil. Handle both shapes.
IgnoreExecutor matters: without it you will match your own closures.

fireclickdetector.name: fireclickdetector
fireclickdetector.signature: function fireclickdetector(detector: ClickDetector, distance: number?, event: string?): ()
fireclickdetector.summary: Triggers a ClickDetector event. By default it fires MouseClick.
fireclickdetector.purpose: Triggers a ClickDetector without a real click, and without being in range. Games often gate interaction behind proximity and a mouse event; this skips both while still going through the game's own handler.
fireclickdetector.example:
local detector = workspace.Door.ClickDetector
fireclickdetector(detector)                    -- default MouseClick
fireclickdetector(detector, 0, "MouseHoverEnter")
gotchas: The event name is case-sensitive and must be one the ClickDetector actually has.
Server-side validation of position still applies; firing locally does not teleport you.

fireproximityprompt.name: fireproximityprompt
fireproximityprompt.summary: Instantly triggers a ProximityPrompt, bypassing its HoldDuration and activation distance.
fireproximityprompt.purpose: Completes a ProximityPrompt instantly, ignoring HoldDuration and MaxActivationDistance. It is the standard way to automate any interact-to-collect mechanic.
fireproximityprompt.example:
for _, prompt in ipairs(workspace:GetDescendants()) do
    if prompt:IsA("ProximityPrompt") then
        fireproximityprompt(prompt)
    end
end
gotchas: Firing every prompt in a loop is the fastest way to get flagged by a server that counts interactions.

firesignal.name: firesignal
firesignal.summary: Invokes all Luau connections attached to a given RBXScriptSignal.
firesignal.purpose: Invokes every Lua listener on a signal without the event that normally triggers it. That means you can make the game react as though something happened — a part was touched, a value changed — purely on the client.
firesignal.example:
-- Trigger every listener on a signal with your own arguments
firesignal(someRemoteEvent.OnClientEvent, "payload")
gotchas: Fires client-side listeners only. The server sees nothing, which is the single most common misunderstanding here.
Argument types are not validated; listeners that expect an Instance and get a string will error.

firetouchinterest.name: firetouchinterest
firetouchinterest.signature: function firetouchinterest(part1: BasePart, part2: BasePart, toggle: boolean | number): ()
firetouchinterest.summary: Simulates a physical touch event between two BaseParts. Can emulate both the start and the end of a Touched event.
firetouchinterest.purpose: Simulates one part touching another, producing the Touched and TouchEnded events the game listens for. Physical contact is normally required; this produces the event without moving anything.
firetouchinterest.example:
local root = game.Players.LocalPlayer.Character.HumanoidRootPart
firetouchinterest(root, workspace.Coin, 0)   -- touch
firetouchinterest(root, workspace.Coin, 1)   -- untouch
gotchas: Most handlers need both the touch and the untouch to fire, in that order, or they treat you as still standing on the part.
The toggle argument accepts 0/1 or true/false depending on the executor.

get_comm_channel.name: get_comm_channel
get_comm_channel.summary: Returns a BindableEvent. Used in one-way communication between actors.
get_comm_channel.purpose: Retrieves a channel by its identifier from inside the actor, so the actor-side code can fire events back to you.
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Actors are Roblox's parallel Luau containers; behaviour here depends on the game actually using them.

getactors.name: getactors
getactors.summary: Returns a table of actors, not including deleted ones.
getactors.purpose: Lists the Actor instances a game is using for parallel Luau. Games that run logic in parallel keep it out of the main environment entirely, so this is the entry point to reach that code at all.
getactors.example:
for _, actor in ipairs(getactors()) do
    print(actor:GetFullName())
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Actors are Roblox's parallel Luau containers; behaviour here depends on the game actually using them.

getactorthreads.name: getactorthreads
getactorthreads.summary: Returns a table of every thread connected to every actor.
getactorthreads.purpose: Lists every thread running under every actor, which is how you find parallel code that has no reachable script instance.
getactorthreads.example:
for _, thread in ipairs(getactorthreads()) do
    if not isourthread(thread) then
        print(getscriptfromthread(thread))
    end
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Actors are Roblox's parallel Luau containers; behaviour here depends on the game actually using them.

getbspval.name: getbspval
getbspval.summary: Reads a BinaryString property's value, such as Terrain.SmoothGrid or PartOperation.PhysicsData.
getbspval.purpose: Reads BinaryString properties that are unreadable by every other route — Terrain.SmoothGrid, PartOperation.PhysicsData, BinaryStringValue.Value — returning the raw bytes behind them.
getbspval.example:
local data = getbspval(workspace.Terrain, "SmoothGrid")
print(#data, "bytes of terrain data")
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Output is binary; encode it before storing or printing.

getcallbackvalue.name: getcallbackvalue
getcallbackvalue.signature: function getcallbackvalue(object: Instance, property: string): any | nil
getcallbackvalue.summary: Retrieves the assigned callback property on an Instance, such as OnInvoke.
getcallbackvalue.purpose: Callback properties like OnInvoke and OnServerInvoke are write-only in normal Luau: you can assign a handler but never read the one that is already there. This returns it, which is how you inspect or wrap an existing callback instead of destroying it.
getcallbackvalue.example:
local handler = getcallbackvalue(someBindableFunction, "OnInvoke")
print(handler)   -- the function the game assigned
gotchas: Returns nil when no callback is assigned.
The property name must match exactly.

getcallingscript.name: getcallingscript
getcallingscript.summary: Returns the script that triggered the current code execution.
getcallingscript.purpose: Inside a hook, tells you which script triggered the current execution. Where checkcaller answers whether it was you, this answers exactly who it was, which lets a hook treat one script differently from another.
getcallingscript.example:
local old
old = hookmetamethod(game, "__namecall", function(self, ...)
    local caller = getcallingscript()
    if caller and caller.Name == "AntiCheat" then
        return nil   -- silence just that script
    end
    return old(self, ...)
end)
gotchas: Returns nil when the call did not originate from a script, including calls from your executor.

getconnection.name: getconnection
getconnection.summary: Returns a single Connection object connected to a given RBXScriptSignal.
getconnection.purpose: Returns a single connection rather than the whole list, for when a signal has one listener you care about and building a table is wasted work.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

getconnections.name: getconnections
getconnections.summary: Retrieves the Connection objects currently attached to a given RBXScriptSignal.
getconnections.purpose: An RBXScriptSignal normally hides who is listening to it. getconnections returns the connection objects, each of which exposes the listener function and lets you disable, enable or fire it. Turning off a single anti-cheat listener without touching anything else usually starts here.
getconnections.example:
for _, connection in ipairs(getconnections(workspace.ChildAdded)) do
    print(connection.Function)   -- the listener
    connection:Disable()         -- stop it firing, keep it restorable
end
gotchas: Connection objects expose Disable, Enable, Fire and Defer on most executors, but not all of them on every one.
Disable is reversible; Disconnect is not. Prefer Disable while testing.
C-side connections have no readable Function.

getcustomasset.name: getcustomasset
getcustomasset.summary: Returns a content ID (e.g. rbxasset://) usable in Roblox APIs for loading audio, meshes, images and other assets.
getcustomasset.purpose: Turns a file on disk into a content ID Roblox will load, which is how a local image, sound or mesh gets into the game without uploading it to the Roblox website first.
getcustomasset.example:
writefile("logo.png", imageData)
local id = getcustomasset("logo.png")
someImageLabel.Image = id
gotchas: The file must already exist inside the executor's workspace folder.
Only formats Roblox itself supports will load. A valid content ID for an unsupported file silently renders nothing.

getdeletedactors.name: getdeletedactors
getdeletedactors.summary: Returns a table of every deleted actor. Some games delete their actors while running.
getdeletedactors.purpose: Returns actors the game has deleted. Some games delete actors immediately after starting their scripts precisely so the actor cannot be inspected; the scripts keep running.
getdeletedactors.example:
for _, actor in ipairs(getdeletedactors()) do
    print("deleted but live:", actor)
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Actors are Roblox's parallel Luau containers; behaviour here depends on the game actually using them.

getfflag.name: getfflag
getfflag.summary: Returns the value of a Fast Flag.
getfflag.purpose: Reads a Roblox Fast Flag, one of the thousands of internal switches that control engine behaviour. Reading them tells you which engine features are active in the running client.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Flag names are exact and change between Roblox versions.

getfflagtype.name: getfflagtype
getfflagtype.summary: Gets the type of a Fast Flag.
getfflagtype.purpose: Reports whether a flag is a bool, int, string or float, so you pass the right value shape to setfflag.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

getfpscap.name: getfpscap
getfpscap.summary: Returns the FPS cap set by the client.
getfpscap.purpose: Reads the client's current frame rate limit.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

getfunctionhash.name: getfunctionhash
getfunctionhash.summary: Returns the hex-represented SHA-384 hash of a function's instructions and constants.
getfunctionhash.purpose: Produces a hash of a function's instructions and constants, so you can identify a function by what it does rather than by name or address. Games rename and reorder things between updates; a hash gives you a stable fingerprint for the function you actually care about.
getfunctionhash.example:
local hash = getfunctionhash(someModule.criticalCheck)
print(hash)  -- hex SHA-384 of the bytecode and constants

-- Detect that a game update changed this function
if hash ~= KNOWN_HASH then
    warn("target function changed, hooks may be wrong")
end
gotchas: Hashes instructions and constants, not upvalues, so two functions differing only in captured state hash the same.
C closures have no readable bytecode; this is for Lua closures.

getgc.name: getgc
getgc.signature: function getgc(includeTables: boolean?): { AnyTable | AnyFunction | userdata }
getgc.summary: Returns a list of non-dead garbage-collectable values: functions, userdatas, and optionally tables.
getgc.purpose: Returns the live objects the garbage collector is tracking, which in practice means every function and userdata currently alive, and optionally every table. It is the brute-force way to find something when you have no reference to it: the game's internal module table, a callback nobody exposed, a closure created inside a scope you cannot reach.
getgc.example:
for _, object in ipairs(getgc(true)) do  -- true = include tables
    if type(object) == "table" and rawget(object, "PlayerData") then
        print("found the player data table")
    end
end
gotchas: Expensive. Scanning the whole GC in a loop will visibly stutter the game.
Without the includeTables argument you get functions and userdata only, and people spend a long time wondering why their table is missing.
Objects can be collected between finding and using them. Store what you need immediately.

getgenv.name: getgenv
getgenv.summary: Returns the executor's global environment table, shared across all executor-made threads.
getgenv.purpose: Your executor runs each script in its own scope, so a variable in one script is invisible to the next. getgenv returns a table shared by every executor thread, which is how scripts detect that they are already running, expose an API to each other, or store settings that survive a re-execute.
getgenv.example:
-- Guard against running twice
if getgenv().MyScriptLoaded then return end
getgenv().MyScriptLoaded = true

-- Expose configuration another script can read
getgenv().Config = { WalkSpeed = 32 }
gotchas: Shared with every other script the user runs, so use a unique key. Generic names like Config collide.
Persists until the executor unloads, which is why re-executing a script without a guard stacks duplicate loops.

gethiddenproperties.name: gethiddenproperties
gethiddenproperties.summary: Returns a table of every non-scriptable property and its value.
gethiddenproperties.purpose: Dumps every non-scriptable property on an instance at once, which is how you discover what is available instead of guessing property names one at a time.
gethiddenproperties.example:
for name, value in pairs(gethiddenproperties(workspace.Part)) do
    print(name, value)
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

gethiddenproperty.name: gethiddenproperty
gethiddenproperty.signature: function gethiddenproperty(instance: Instance, property_name: string): (any, boolean)
gethiddenproperty.summary: Retrieves the value of a hidden or non-scriptable property (e.g. BinaryString, SharedString, SystemAddress), even if it would normally throw when accessed directly.
gethiddenproperty.purpose: Roblox marks a lot of properties non-scriptable: reading them from Luau throws. They are still there, and often hold exactly what you want — internal flags, binary blobs, network state. This reads them anyway.
gethiddenproperty.example:
local value, isHidden = gethiddenproperty(workspace.Part, "Size")
print(value, isHidden)

-- The interesting case: a property normal code cannot touch at all
print(gethiddenproperty(game.Players.LocalPlayer, "SimulationRadius"))
gotchas: Returns two values. The second tells you whether the property was actually hidden, and people routinely ignore it.
BinaryString and SharedString values come back as raw bytes, not printable text.

gethui.name: gethui
gethui.summary: Returns a hidden Instance container used for safely storing UI elements.
gethui.purpose: Anything you put in PlayerGui is visible to game scripts, which routinely scan it and remove UI they did not create. gethui returns a container the game's scripts cannot see, so your interface survives.
gethui.example:
local gui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
gui.Parent = gethui()   -- instead of PlayerGui
gotchas: Returns a Folder on some executors and a hidden PlayerGui on others. Do not assume the class.
UI parented here still renders normally.

gethwid.name: gethwid
gethwid.summary: Returns a unique string for the user's device.
gethwid.purpose: Returns a string that identifies the machine. Script sellers use it for licence keys tied to a device.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
This is an identifier for the user's own machine. Treat it as sensitive: do not log or transmit it without the user knowing.

getinstances.name: getinstances
getinstances.summary: Retrieves every Instance from the registry, including ones that are or were parented to nil.
getinstances.purpose: game:GetDescendants only sees what is parented into the DataModel. getinstances reads the engine's own instance registry, so it also returns objects that were removed, hidden or never parented — which is where games routinely put things they do not want a client to find.
getinstances.example:
for _, inst in ipairs(getinstances()) do
    if inst:IsA("RemoteEvent") and not inst.Parent then
        print("orphaned remote:", inst.Name)
    end
end
gotchas: Returns a very large table in most games. Filter as you iterate rather than copying it.
Includes destroyed instances that have not been collected yet.

getloadedmodules.name: getloadedmodules
getloadedmodules.summary: Returns every ModuleScript that has been loaded (require'd).
getloadedmodules.purpose: Returns every ModuleScript the game has already required. Games keep most of their logic in modules, so this is usually a shorter and more relevant list than getscripts when you are looking for game code.
getloadedmodules.example:
for _, module in ipairs(getloadedmodules()) do
    print(module:GetFullName())
end
gotchas: Only modules already required. A module loaded later will not appear until it is.

getnamecallmethod.name: getnamecallmethod
getnamecallmethod.summary: Returns the name of the method that invoked the __namecall metamethod.
getnamecallmethod.purpose: __namecall fires for every method call in the game, but the metamethod itself does not tell you which method was invoked. getnamecallmethod does, and without it a __namecall hook cannot distinguish FireServer from GetChildren.
getnamecallmethod.example:
local old
old = hookmetamethod(game, "__namecall", function(self, ...)
    local method = getnamecallmethod()
    if method == "InvokeServer" and not checkcaller() then
        print("game invoked", self.Name)
    end
    return old(self, ...)
end)
gotchas: Only meaningful inside a __namecall hook. Outside one it returns nothing useful.
Compare the method name case-sensitively; it is the exact method identifier.

getnilinstances.name: getnilinstances
getnilinstances.summary: Returns Instances that are currently unparented. They exist in memory but are no longer part of the DataModel hierarchy.
getnilinstances.purpose: Narrows getinstances to objects with no parent. Scripts that want to stay out of reach commonly set Parent to nil while keeping a reference, and this is the list that exposes them.
getnilinstances.example:
for _, inst in ipairs(getnilinstances()) do
    if inst:IsA("LocalScript") then
        print("hidden script:", inst.Name)
    end
end
gotchas: An instance parented to nil is still running if it was started before being unparented.

getobjects.name: getobjects
getobjects.summary: Equivalent to game:GetObjects, fetching an asset from Roblox.
getobjects.purpose: Fetches an asset from Roblox by ID and returns it as instances, the executor's version of game:GetObjects, which is normally restricted on the client.
gotchas: Yields while downloading.
Returns a table, even for a single asset.

getpcd.name: getpcd
getpcd.summary: Returns a 16-byte hash and binary data for a TriangleMeshPart's PhysicalConfigData property.
getpcd.purpose: Returns the hash and binary payload of a TriangleMeshPart's PhysicalConfigData, the collision geometry description that is otherwise entirely opaque to scripts.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

getproperties.name: getproperties
getproperties.summary: Returns a table of every property, including non-scriptable ones, and its value.
getproperties.purpose: Returns every property on an instance, scriptable and hidden together, giving you the full picture of an object's state in one call.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Large for complex instances; do not call it per frame.

getproximitypromptduration.name: getproximitypromptduration
getproximitypromptduration.summary: Returns the value of a proximity prompt's duration.
getproximitypromptduration.purpose: Reads a prompt's hold duration, including when the property has been made non-scriptable, so tooling can restore the original value after changing it.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

getrawmetatable.name: getrawmetatable
getrawmetatable.signature: function getrawmetatable(object: { any } | userdata): { [any]: any } | nil
getrawmetatable.summary: Returns the raw metatable of an object, even if that object has a __metatable field set.
getrawmetatable.purpose: Roblox locks its objects' metatables by setting __metatable, so getmetatable returns a string instead of the real table. getrawmetatable ignores that lock and hands you the actual metatable, which is the entry point for reading or hooking __index and __namecall.
getrawmetatable.example:
local mt = getrawmetatable(game)
print(getmetatable(game))   -- "The metatable is locked"
print(typeof(mt))           -- "table", the real one

setreadonly(mt, false)      -- metatables are readonly until you unlock them
local oldIndex = mt.__index
mt.__index = newcclosure(function(self, key)
    return oldIndex(self, key)
end)
setreadonly(mt, true)
gotchas: The returned metatable is readonly. Writing to it without setreadonly(mt, false) errors.
Every Roblox instance shares one metatable, so a change affects the entire game, not just the object you passed.
Leaving the metatable unlocked is itself a detectable state. Lock it again when you are done.

getreg.name: getreg
getreg.summary: Returns the Luau registry table, used internally to store references shared between C and Luau.
getreg.purpose: The Luau registry is where the C side of the engine keeps strong references to things it needs to survive garbage collection: threads, callbacks, userdata. Reading it is a way to find objects that are not reachable from any Lua variable you can see.
getreg.example:
for _, value in pairs(getreg()) do
    if type(value) == "thread" then
        print("live thread:", value)
    end
end
gotchas: Anything in the registry is never collected, so treat it as read-mostly. Writing here leaks memory permanently.
The table is large. Iterate with a filter rather than dumping it.

getrenderproperty.name: getrenderproperty
getrenderproperty.signature: function getrenderproperty(drawing: Drawing, property: string): any
getrenderproperty.summary: Retrieves the value of a property from a Drawing object. Behaves identically to object[property], but is useful for dynamic property names or reflection-like access.
getrenderproperty.purpose: Reads a drawing property by name rather than by field access, which is what generic code needs when the property is decided at runtime.
gotchas: Behaves the same as box.Visible; the value is in the dynamic name, not the mechanism.

getrendersteppedlist.name: getrendersteppedlist
getrendersteppedlist.summary: Returns a table of every callback bound using BindToRenderStep.
getrendersteppedlist.purpose: RunService:BindToRenderStep hides its callbacks entirely — there is no way to enumerate them in normal code. This returns them, so you can see what runs every frame and, if needed, replace one.
getrendersteppedlist.example:
for name, callback in pairs(getrendersteppedlist()) do
    print(name, callback)
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

getrenv.name: getrenv
getrenv.summary: Returns the Roblox global environment used by the game. Changes to it affect your executor environment as well.
getrenv.purpose: Returns the game's own global environment, the one every Roblox script sees. Reading it shows you the globals the game has defined; writing to it changes what game scripts see, which is a blunt but effective way to replace a global function everywhere at once.
getrenv.example:
local renv = getrenv()
print(renv.game == game)   -- the game's own reference

-- See what globals the game added
for key, value in pairs(renv) do
    if type(value) == "function" then
        print(key)
    end
end
gotchas: This is the game's environment, not yours. Changes affect game scripts and are highly visible.
getrenv().print is not the same object as your print; hooking one does not hook the other.

getrunningscripts.name: getrunningscripts
getrunningscripts.summary: Returns all running scripts in the caller's global state, excluding CoreScripts by default.
getrunningscripts.purpose: Narrows the list to scripts that are currently executing, which is the set that actually has an environment you can read with getsenv. CoreScripts are excluded by default.
getrunningscripts.example:
for _, s in ipairs(getrunningscripts()) do
    local env = getsenv(s)
    if env and env.PlayerData then
        print("found state in", s:GetFullName())
    end
end
gotchas: A script that has finished running no longer appears here even though the instance still exists.

getscriptbytecode.name: getscriptbytecode
getscriptbytecode.signature: function getscriptbytecode(script: BaseScript | ModuleScript): string | nil
getscriptbytecode.summary: Retrieves the compiled bytecode of a Script, LocalScript or ModuleScript.
getscriptbytecode.purpose: Hands you a script's compiled bytecode as a string. Roblox never ships Luau source to the client, so bytecode is the closest thing to source that exists on your machine, and it is the input to every decompiler and analysis tool.
getscriptbytecode.example:
local target = game:GetService("Players").LocalPlayer.PlayerScripts.Main
local bytecode = getscriptbytecode(target)
print(#bytecode, "bytes")
gotchas: Returns nil for scripts whose bytecode is not available on the client, including many server-side scripts.
The result is binary, not text. Base64 it before writing it anywhere that expects a string.

getscriptclosure.name: getscriptclosure
getscriptclosure.summary: Creates and returns a Luau closure from a script's compiled bytecode.
getscriptclosure.purpose: Turns a script's bytecode back into a callable function, giving you the script's main body as a closure you can inspect with the debug library — its constants, its protos, its structure — without running the game's copy.
getscriptclosure.example:
local closure = getscriptclosure(someModuleScript)
-- Inspect what the module references
for _, constant in ipairs(debug.getconstants(closure)) do
    print(constant)
end
gotchas: The returned closure is a fresh instance. Calling it runs the script body again, which is rarely what you want.
Commonly used for reading a ModuleScript's return table without triggering the game's own require.

getscriptfromthread.name: getscriptfromthread
getscriptfromthread.signature: function getscriptfromthread(thread: thread): BaseScript | ModuleScript | nil
getscriptfromthread.summary: Returns the script associated with a given Luau thread.
getscriptfromthread.purpose: Maps a running thread back to the script that owns it, which is how you make sense of a thread list from the registry or from an actor.
getscriptfromthread.example:
local s = getscriptfromthread(coroutine.running())
print(s and s:GetFullName() or "not a script thread")
gotchas: Returns nil for threads with no owning script, including your own.

getscripthash.name: getscripthash
getscripthash.signature: function getscripthash(script: BaseScript | ModuleScript): string | nil
getscripthash.summary: Returns a hexadecimal SHA-384 hash of a script's raw bytecode.
getscripthash.purpose: A SHA-384 fingerprint of a script's bytecode. Because the hash changes whenever the script changes, it is how tooling detects that a game updated and that offsets, constant indices or hooks need revisiting.
getscripthash.example:
local hash = getscripthash(script)
if hash ~= SAVED_HASH then
    warn("script changed since this was written")
end
gotchas: Hex-encoded string, not raw bytes.
Returns nil when bytecode is unavailable.

getscripts.name: getscripts
getscripts.summary: Returns every Script, LocalScript and ModuleScript instance present.
getscripts.purpose: Lists every script instance in the game, including ones parented to nil that a normal descendant search would never find. It is the starting point for locating the script you actually want to inspect.
getscripts.example:
for _, s in ipairs(getscripts()) do
    if s.Name == "AntiCheat" then
        print(s:GetFullName())
    end
end
gotchas: Includes scripts that are not running. Cross-check with getrunningscripts if you need a live environment.

getscriptthread.name: getscriptthread
getscriptthread.summary: Returns the thread derived from an associated script, or nil.
getscriptthread.purpose: The inverse mapping: given a script, hand back the thread it is running on. Useful when you want to inspect or manipulate a specific script's execution rather than search a list of threads.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Returns nil if the script is not currently running.

getsenv.name: getsenv
getsenv.signature: function getsenv(script: BaseScript | ModuleScript): { [any]: any } | nil
getsenv.summary: Returns the global environment table of a given Script, LocalScript or ModuleScript.
getsenv.purpose: Gives you the environment table of one specific script, which means direct access to that script's local-looking globals and its functions. When you want to call a game function that was never exposed anywhere, this is usually how you reach it.
getsenv.example:
local script = game:GetService("Players").LocalPlayer.PlayerScripts.MainScript
local env = getsenv(script)

for key, value in pairs(env) do
    print(key, typeof(value))
end

env.someInternalFunction()  -- call it directly
gotchas: Only works on a script that is actually running. A script that has not started, or has finished, has no environment.
Returns nil rather than erroring in most implementations, so check the result.
Reaching into a script's environment does not make its true locals visible; only its globals and function environment.

getsignalarguments.name: getsignalarguments
getsignalarguments.summary: Returns a table of expected argument types for a given RBXScriptSignal.
getsignalarguments.purpose: Reports the argument types a signal expects. Since replicatesignal fails on a type mismatch, this is how you find out what to pass without trial and error.
getsignalarguments.example:
for i, argType in ipairs(getsignalarguments(prompt.Triggered)) do
    print(i, argType)
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

getsignalargumentsinfo.name: getsignalargumentsinfo
getsignalargumentsinfo.summary: Returns a table of expected argument information for a given RBXScriptSignal, usable for replicating signals.
getsignalargumentsinfo.purpose: The detailed form of getsignalarguments, returning per-argument information rather than bare type names, which is what you need to construct a valid replicated call.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.

getsignalwhitelist.name: getsignalwhitelist
getsignalwhitelist.summary: Returns a table of SignalWhitelistInfo objects in Roblox's replication whitelist.
getsignalwhitelist.purpose: Lists the signals Roblox permits clients to replicate. It answers 'what can I actually fire to the server' once, instead of testing signals one at a time.
getsignalwhitelist.example:
for _, entry in ipairs(getsignalwhitelist()) do
    print(entry.ClassName, entry.SignalName)
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
The whitelist changes with Roblox updates.

getsimulationradius.name: getsimulationradius
getsimulationradius.summary: Returns the simulation radius of the LocalPlayer.
getsimulationradius.purpose: Reads how far from your character the client is responsible for simulating physics. Network ownership follows this radius, so it decides which parts you can move directly rather than requesting the server move them.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Roblox has tightened server-side checks on this over time; a large local value is not authoritative.

gettenv.name: gettenv
gettenv.purpose: Returns the environment of a specific thread rather than a script. Threads created by coroutine.create or by the engine can carry their own environment, and this is how you inspect one you pulled out of the registry or from an actor.
gettenv.example:
local thread = coroutine.create(function() end)
local env = gettenv(thread)
print(env.print == print)
gotchas: Potassium-specific; sUNC does not test this.

getthreadidentity.name: getthreadidentity
getthreadidentity.summary: Retrieves the thread identity of the running Luau thread.
getthreadidentity.purpose: Roblox gates what code can do behind an identity level: what services it can reach, which properties it can write, whether it can call protected APIs. Reading the current identity explains why a call that works in one context errors in another.
getthreadidentity.example: print(getthreadidentity())   -- commonly 8 in an executor thread
gotchas: Identity is per-thread. A new coroutine may not inherit what you expect.
Some executors report a spoofed value; behaviour is the real test, which is exactly what sUNC checks.

hookfunction.name: hookfunction
hookfunction.summary: Replaces a function's behaviour with another function, returning the original unhooked function.
hookfunction.purpose: Every script eventually reaches a point where the game already has a function that does the thing you want to change, and rewriting it is not an option because the game calls its own copy. hookfunction swaps the body of that existing function for yours, so every existing call site now runs your code instead. It returns the original, which is how you keep the old behaviour available.
hookfunction.example:
-- Keep a reference to the game's function
local target = someModule.getWalkSpeed

-- Replace it. `original` is the untouched version.
local original
original = hookfunction(target, function(...)
    -- Call the original whenever you want the real result
    local result = original(...)
    print("getWalkSpeed returned", result)
    return result
end)
gotchas: Always call the stored original, never the hooked name, or you will call yourself and stack overflow.
Hooking a C function with a Lua function has argument-count and closure-type limits on many executors. Wrap your hook in newcclosure when the target is a C closure.
The upvalue count of your hook must not exceed the target's on some implementations; hook a small wrapper instead of a large closure.

hookmetamethod.name: hookmetamethod
hookmetamethod.signature: function hookmetamethod(object: { [any]: any } | Instance | userdata, metamethodName: string, hook: (...any) -> (...any)): (...any) -> (...any)
hookmetamethod.summary: Hooks a specific metamethod of an object that has a metatable. Internally it uses hookfunction on that metamethod.
hookmetamethod.purpose: Roblox objects route almost everything through metamethods: indexing a property goes through __index, calling a method goes through __namecall. Hooking one of those is how you intercept every property read or every remote call in the game at once, instead of hunting for individual functions. It is hookfunction aimed at the metatable, with the unlocking handled for you.
hookmetamethod.example:
local mt = getrawmetatable(game)

-- Intercept every method call in the game (`obj:Method(...)`)
local oldNamecall
oldNamecall = hookmetamethod(game, "__namecall", function(self, ...)
    local method = getnamecallmethod()  -- which method was called
    if method == "FireServer" then
        print("FireServer on", self:GetFullName(), ...)
    end
    return oldNamecall(self, ...)       -- let the real call continue
end)
gotchas: Your hook runs for the entire game, including your own calls. Guard with checkcaller so you do not intercept yourself.
Never yield inside a __index or __namecall hook. It runs on the game's thread and yielding there breaks the caller.
Returning the wrong number of values changes behaviour for every caller in the game, not just the one you were targeting.

httpget.name: httpget
httpget.summary: Performs an HTTP GET request to a URL.
httpget.purpose: A shorthand for a GET request that returns the body as a string. It is what game:HttpGet wraps, and what the standard loadstring(game:HttpGet(url))() pattern relies on.
gotchas: Yields.
No status code is returned, so a 404 page arrives as a perfectly valid string.

identifyexecutor.name: identifyexecutor
identifyexecutor.summary: Returns the name and version of the currently running executor.
identifyexecutor.purpose: Returns the name and version of the environment your script is running in. Scripts use it to branch around implementation differences, since no two executors implement the standard identically.
identifyexecutor.example:
local name, version = identifyexecutor()
print(name, version)

if name == "Potassium" then
    -- use a Potassium-only path
end
gotchas: Returns two values on sUNC-compliant implementations; some older ones return only a name.
Trivially spoofable, so treat it as a hint, not proof.

is_parallel.name: is_parallel
is_parallel.summary: Returns a boolean indicating whether is_parallel was called in parallel.
is_parallel.purpose: Reports whether the calling code is executing in parallel. Parallel contexts forbid most writes to the DataModel, so this tells you which operations are legal right now.
is_parallel.example:
if is_parallel() then
    warn("cannot write to the DataModel here")
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Actors are Roblox's parallel Luau containers; behaviour here depends on the game actually using them.

iscclosure.name: iscclosure
iscclosure.summary: Checks whether a given function is a C closure.
iscclosure.purpose: Tells you whether a function was defined in C (the engine, or your executor's own natives) or compiled from Luau source. This matters constantly when hooking, because C functions and Lua functions have different hooking rules and different failure modes.
iscclosure.example:
print(iscclosure(print))          -- true, engine-defined
print(iscclosure(function() end)) -- false, compiled from source
gotchas: iscclosure and islclosure should always disagree for a valid function. If both return true, the implementation is fake.

isexecutorclosure.name: isexecutorclosure
isexecutorclosure.summary: Checks whether a given function is a closure created by the executor, including ones from getscriptclosure or loadstring.
isexecutorclosure.purpose: Separates functions your executor created from functions the game created. This is the check anti-cheat authors wish they had, and the check you use to make sure a callback you found in the GC is actually yours before you modify it.
isexecutorclosure.example:
print(isexecutorclosure(print))                    -- false, engine
print(isexecutorclosure(function() end))           -- true, yours
print(isexecutorclosure(loadstring("return 1")))   -- true, compiled by the executor
gotchas: Must be true for closures from loadstring and getscriptclosure, not only for literal functions in your script. sUNC checks both.

isfile.name: isfile
isfile.summary: Checks whether a given path exists and refers to a file.
isfile.purpose: Checks a path exists and is a file, which is the guard that keeps readfile from erroring. Nearly every filesystem bug in exploit scripts is a missing isfile check.
isfile.example:
if not isfile("myscript/config.json") then
    writefile("myscript/config.json", "{}")
end
gotchas: Returns false for folders, so a path that exists can still return false.

isfolder.name: isfolder
isfolder.summary: Checks whether a given path exists and refers to a folder.
isfolder.purpose: The folder equivalent of isfile, used before makefolder so you do not recreate a directory you already have.
isfolder.example:
if not isfolder("myscript") then
    makefolder("myscript")
end

isfunctionhooked.name: isfunctionhooked
isfunctionhooked.summary: Returns a boolean indicating whether the function has been hooked.
isfunctionhooked.purpose: Lets you check whether a function has already been replaced before you hook it yourself, which prevents you from chaining onto another script's hook by accident or double-hooking on a script re-run.
isfunctionhooked.example:
if not isfunctionhooked(target) then
    original = hookfunction(target, myHook)
end
gotchas: Only knows about hooks made through your executor's own hooking functions.

islclosure.name: islclosure
islclosure.summary: Checks whether a given function is a Luau closure.
islclosure.purpose: The complement of iscclosure: it reports whether a function is a Luau closure compiled from source. Use it to confirm a value you pulled out of the garbage collector or a script environment is real game code before you try to read its constants or upvalues.
islclosure.example:
local fn = function() return 1 end
if islclosure(fn) then
    -- only Lua closures have readable constants and protos
    print(#debug.getconstants(fn))
end
gotchas: debug library functions that read bytecode fail or error on C closures. Check with islclosure first.

isnetworkowner.name: isnetworkowner
isnetworkowner.summary: Returns whether the LocalPlayer is the network owner of a given instance.
isnetworkowner.purpose: Answers whether your client, rather than the server, is currently simulating a given part. It is the check that decides whether directly setting a part's CFrame will actually replicate.
isnetworkowner.example:
if isnetworkowner(workspace.Ball) then
    workspace.Ball.Velocity = Vector3.new(0, 100, 0)
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Ownership changes as parts move in and out of your simulation radius.

isnewcclosure.name: isnewcclosure
isnewcclosure.summary: Returns a boolean indicating whether the function has been created using newcclosure.
isnewcclosure.purpose: Reports whether a function is a wrapper produced by newcclosure rather than a genuine C closure. It exists because the wrapper is supposed to be indistinguishable, and this is how you check your own work: if game code can tell, so can an implementation of this function.
isnewcclosure.example:
local wrapped = newcclosure(function() end)
print(iscclosure(wrapped))      -- true, reports as C
print(isnewcclosure(wrapped))   -- true, but it is a wrapper
gotchas: Potassium-specific; not part of the sUNC standard.
Returns false for real C closures such as print.

isourthread.name: isourthread
isourthread.summary: Returns a boolean indicating whether the thread is a Potassium thread.
isourthread.purpose: A thread-level version of checkcaller: it reports whether a given thread belongs to the executor rather than the game. Useful when you are inspecting a list of threads (from an actor, or from the registry) and need to filter your own out.
isourthread.example:
for _, thread in ipairs(getactorthreads()) do
    if not isourthread(thread) then
        print("game thread:", thread)
    end
end
gotchas: Distinct from checkcaller, which always asks about the currently running thread.

isrbxactive.name: isrbxactive
isrbxactive.summary: Returns a boolean indicating whether Roblox is currently in focus.
isrbxactive.purpose: Reports whether the Roblox window currently has focus. Every simulated input function silently does nothing when it does not, so this is the check that explains why an automation script 'stopped working' the moment you alt-tabbed.
isrbxactive.example:
if isrbxactive() then
    keytap(0x20)   -- space
end
gotchas: Named isrbxactive on most executors; some also expose it as iswindowactive.

isreadonly.name: isreadonly
isreadonly.summary: Checks whether a table is currently set as readonly.
isreadonly.purpose: Checks the readonly flag before you write to a table, so you can restore the exact previous state instead of blindly locking or unlocking. Useful in library code that must not leave the environment different from how it found it.
isreadonly.example:
local wasReadonly = isreadonly(mt)
setreadonly(mt, false)
-- ... edit ...
setreadonly(mt, wasReadonly)  -- restore whatever it was

isrenderobj.name: isrenderobj
isrenderobj.summary: Checks whether a given value is a valid Drawing object.
isrenderobj.purpose: Checks that a value is a live drawing object before you touch it, which matters because a removed drawing still looks like a table.
isrenderobj.example:
if isrenderobj(box) then
    box.Visible = false
end

isscriptable.name: isscriptable
isscriptable.signature: function isscriptable(object: Instance, property: string): boolean | nil
isscriptable.summary: Returns whether the given property of an Instance is scriptable (i.e. it does not have the notscriptable tag).
isscriptable.purpose: Tells you whether a property can be read and written through ordinary indexing. Checking first is how you decide between a plain read and a hidden-property read.
isscriptable.example:
if isscriptable(workspace.Part, "Size") then
    print(workspace.Part.Size)
else
    print(gethiddenproperty(workspace.Part, "Size"))
end
gotchas: Returns nil, not false, when the property does not exist at all.

keypress.name: keypress
keypress.summary: Simulates a key being pressed, only while Roblox is in focus.
keypress.purpose: Holds a key down at the OS level, so the game receives it as a real key press rather than a synthesised Roblox input. Pair it with keyrelease for anything that needs to be held.
keypress.example:
keypress(0x57)      -- hold W
task.wait(1)
keyrelease(0x57)    -- let go
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.
Takes a virtual key code, not a Roblox KeyCode enum.
A keypress with no matching keyrelease leaves the key stuck down.

keyrelease.name: keyrelease
keyrelease.summary: Simulates a key being released, only while Roblox is in focus.
keyrelease.purpose: Releases a key held with keypress. Every hold needs one, or the game keeps seeing the key as down after your script ends.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.

keytap.name: keytap
keytap.summary: Simulates a key being pressed and released, only while Roblox is in focus.
keytap.purpose: A press and release in one call, for keys that only need a momentary tap.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.

listfiles.name: listfiles
listfiles.summary: Returns an array of strings representing all files and folders within the specified directory.
listfiles.purpose: Enumerates a directory, returning full paths for the files and folders inside. It is how a script discovers what it saved earlier without hardcoding names.
listfiles.example:
for _, path in ipairs(listfiles("myscript")) do
    if isfile(path) then
        print(path)
    end
end
gotchas: Returns full relative paths, not bare names.
Not recursive. Walk into subfolders yourself.

loadfile.name: loadfile
loadfile.signature: function loadfile<A...>(path: string): ((A...) -> any | nil, string?)
loadfile.summary: Compiles the Luau source in a file and returns the resulting chunk, which runs in the global environment.
loadfile.purpose: Compiles a file on disk into a runnable chunk without executing it, so you can inspect or conditionally run stored code. It is loadstring with a path instead of a string.
loadfile.example:
local chunk, err = loadfile("myscript/module.lua")
if chunk then
    local result = chunk()
end
gotchas: Returns nil plus an error message on a compile failure, exactly like loadstring.
Does not run the chunk. Use dofile if that is what you meant.

loadstring.name: loadstring
loadstring.signature: function loadstring<A...>(source: string, chunkname: string?): (((A...) -> any) | nil, string?)
loadstring.summary: Compiles a string of Luau code into a runnable function, or returns nil plus an error message.
loadstring.purpose: Compiles Luau source at runtime. Roblox disables this in normal game code, so its presence is one of the defining features of an executor environment. It is what every loadstring(game:HttpGet(...))() one-liner depends on.
loadstring.example:
local chunk, err = loadstring("return 2 + 2")
if not chunk then
    warn("compile error:", err)
    return
end
print(chunk())  -- 4
gotchas: Returns nil plus an error string on a compile error rather than throwing. Check the first return value.
A compile error is not a runtime error. Wrap the call to the chunk in pcall separately.
The chunk runs in the global environment, not in your script's scope.

lz4compress.name: lz4compress
lz4compress.summary: Compresses a string with the LZ4 compression algorithm.
lz4compress.purpose: Compresses a string with LZ4, which is fast enough to use on data you are about to write or send without a noticeable pause. Bytecode and repetitive JSON shrink dramatically.
gotchas: Output is binary. Base64 it if it needs to be text.
Only lz4decompress can read it; this is not gzip or zlib.
lz4compress.alias_note: Same function under two names: `lz4compress` in the sUNC standard, `crypt.lz4compress` in Potassium.

lz4decompress.name: lz4decompress
lz4decompress.summary: Decompresses an LZ4-compressed string back to regular data.
lz4decompress.purpose: Restores LZ4-compressed data. Some implementations require you to know the original size, which is why people commonly store it alongside the payload.
gotchas: Certain executors take a second argument for the decompressed size and fail without it.
lz4decompress.alias_note: Same function under two names: `lz4decompress` in the sUNC standard, `crypt.lz4decompress` in Potassium.

makefolder.name: makefolder
makefolder.summary: Creates a folder at the specified path if one does not already exist.
makefolder.purpose: Creates a directory in the workspace folder. Since writefile will not create parent folders for you, this is the first call in almost every script that stores anything.
makefolder.example:
makefolder("myscript")
makefolder("myscript/cache")   -- create nested paths one level at a time
gotchas: Nested creation in a single call is not reliable across executors. Create each level.

makereadonly.name: makereadonly
makereadonly.purpose: A named shorthand for locking a table, equivalent to setreadonly(t, true). Potassium exposes the two directions as separate calls, which reads more clearly in code that locks and unlocks repeatedly.
gotchas: Potassium naming. Scripts written for the sUNC standard use setreadonly instead.

makewritable.name: makewritable
makewritable.purpose: The unlock half of the pair, equivalent to setreadonly(t, false). Same behaviour, clearer intent at the call site.
gotchas: Potassium naming. Scripts written for the sUNC standard use setreadonly instead.

messagebox.name: messagebox
messagebox.summary: Creates a message box with the specified text, caption and flags.
messagebox.purpose: Opens a native OS dialog with a message and buttons, and yields until the user answers. Useful for a confirmation that must not be missed, since in-game UI can be covered or removed.
messagebox.example:
local result = messagebox("Continue?", "My Script", 4)  -- 4 = Yes/No
print(result)
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Blocks the calling thread until dismissed.
Flag values follow the Win32 MessageBox constants.

mouse1click.name: mouse1click
mouse1click.summary: Simulates a left mouse click, only while Roblox is in focus.
mouse1click.purpose: A full left click at the current cursor position, delivered as a real OS input.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.

mouse1press.name: mouse1press
mouse1press.summary: Simulates a left mouse press, only while Roblox is in focus.
mouse1press.purpose: Presses and holds the left mouse button, for click-and-drag or hold-to-fire behaviour.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.
An unmatched press leaves the button held down.

mouse1release.name: mouse1release
mouse1release.summary: Simulates a left mouse release, only while Roblox is in focus.
mouse1release.purpose: Releases a held left mouse button.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.

mouse2click.name: mouse2click
mouse2click.summary: Simulates a right mouse click, only while Roblox is in focus.
mouse2click.purpose: A full right click at the current cursor position.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.

mouse2press.name: mouse2press
mouse2press.summary: Simulates a right mouse press, only while Roblox is in focus.
mouse2press.purpose: Presses and holds the right mouse button, which in Roblox is also how camera rotation starts.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.

mouse2release.name: mouse2release
mouse2release.summary: Simulates a right mouse release, only while Roblox is in focus.
mouse2release.purpose: Releases a held right mouse button.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.

mousemoveabs.name: mousemoveabs
mousemoveabs.summary: Simulates a mouse movement to an absolute screen position.
mousemoveabs.purpose: Moves the cursor to an absolute screen position. Use it when you have a screen coordinate, such as the projected position of a world point.
mousemoveabs.example:
local viewport = workspace.CurrentCamera.ViewportSize
mousemoveabs(viewport.X / 2, viewport.Y / 2)   -- centre of screen
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.
Coordinates are screen pixels, not Roblox GUI offsets, and the two differ with display scaling.

mousemoverel.name: mousemoverel
mousemoverel.summary: Simulates a mouse movement relative to the current mouse position.
mousemoverel.purpose: Moves the cursor by an offset from where it is now. Relative movement is what camera control needs, since the camera responds to deltas rather than positions.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.
Large deltas in one call read as a jump; step them for smooth movement.

mousescroll.name: mousescroll
mousescroll.summary: Simulates a mouse scroll, only while Roblox is in focus.
mousescroll.purpose: Simulates a scroll wheel movement, which in Roblox usually means zooming the camera.
gotchas: Input is only delivered while the Roblox window is focused. If nothing happens, check isrbxactive first.

newcclosure.name: newcclosure
newcclosure.summary: Takes any Luau function and wraps it into a C closure.
newcclosure.purpose: Lua closures and C closures are distinguishable at runtime, and game code can check which one it holds. If you hand a plain Lua function to something that expects a C function, that difference is visible. newcclosure wraps your Lua function so it reports as a C closure while still running your Luau code.
newcclosure.example:
local myHook = function(...)
    return "intercepted"
end

print(iscclosure(myHook))                -- false, plain Lua closure
local wrapped = newcclosure(myHook)
print(iscclosure(wrapped))               -- true, now indistinguishable by type
print(isnewcclosure(wrapped))            -- true on executors that expose this
gotchas: Wrapped functions historically could not yield. Modern implementations allow it, but do not assume it on every executor.
Wrapping is not free. Do not call newcclosure inside a hot loop or a hook body; wrap once and reuse.
A poor implementation leaks the wrapper through error messages or debug.info. sUNC tests exactly this.

newlclosure.name: newlclosure
newlclosure.summary: Creates a new Lua closure for func.
newlclosure.purpose: The inverse of newcclosure. It wraps a function so it reports as a Lua closure, which matters when code checks that a callback is Lua-defined before accepting it, or when a C closure would be rejected by a check that expects game-authored code.
newlclosure.example:
local cfn = print                 -- a C closure
local asLua = newlclosure(cfn)

print(iscclosure(cfn))            -- true
print(islclosure(asLua))          -- true
gotchas: Less widely implemented than newcclosure. Check for it before relying on it.
Wrapping does not change what the function does, only how it identifies.

oth.get_original_thread.name: oth.get_original_thread
oth.get_original_thread.summary: Returns the original thread a hook comes from, or nil if the current thread is not a hook.
oth.get_original_thread.purpose: Gives you the thread that triggered the hook, so you can inspect the real caller's context from your isolated thread.
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Off-thread hooking exists because a hook running on the caller's own thread is comparatively easy to notice.
Returns nil when the current thread is not a hook thread.

oth.get_root_callback.name: oth.get_root_callback
oth.get_root_callback.summary: Retrieves a function that calls the original function in the context of a hook thread.
oth.get_root_callback.purpose: Returns a callable that invokes the original function from inside a hook thread. Because the hook body is not on the original thread, you cannot simply call a saved reference.
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Off-thread hooking exists because a hook running on the caller's own thread is comparatively easy to notice.
Only valid inside a hook thread.

oth.hook.name: oth.hook
oth.hook.summary: Hooks a function using an off-thread execution model that runs hook code on isolated threads.
oth.hook.purpose: Hooks a function so your hook body runs on an isolated thread rather than the caller's. It is aimed at C functions, where an ordinary hookfunction is more constrained and more visible.
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Off-thread hooking exists because a hook running on the caller's own thread is comparatively easy to notice.
Inside the hook you are on a different thread, so checkcaller and thread identity read differently than you expect.

oth.is_hook_thread.name: oth.is_hook_thread
oth.is_hook_thread.summary: Returns whether or not the current thread is a hook thread.
oth.is_hook_thread.purpose: Checks whether the code is currently running inside an off-thread hook, which the other oth functions require.
oth.is_hook_thread.example:
if oth.is_hook_thread() then
    local original = oth.get_root_callback()
end
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Off-thread hooking exists because a hook running on the caller's own thread is comparatively easy to notice.

oth.unhook.name: oth.unhook
oth.unhook.summary: Unhooks a function previously hooked with oth.hook.
oth.unhook.purpose: Removes an off-thread hook, restoring the original function.
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Off-thread hooking exists because a hook running on the caller's own thread is comparatively easy to notice.

queueonteleport.name: queueonteleport
queueonteleport.summary: Queues code for teleport, executing it once a teleport completes.
queueonteleport.purpose: Stores code to run automatically after the next teleport. Executed scripts do not survive a place change, so without this every hub-to-game teleport means re-running your script by hand.
gotchas: The queued code is a string, so it cannot capture any of your current variables.
It runs on arrival in the new place, before the game's own scripts have necessarily finished loading.

raknet.add_receive_hook.name: raknet.add_receive_hook
raknet.add_receive_hook.summary: Registers a callback that runs before a RakNetPacket is received.
raknet.add_receive_hook.purpose: Registers a callback that runs before an incoming packet is processed, letting you observe what the server sent before the engine acts on it.
gotchas: Potassium-specific, and the lowest-level surface in the environment: you are handling raw network packets rather than Roblox objects.

raknet.add_send_hook.name: raknet.add_send_hook
raknet.add_send_hook.summary: Registers a callback that runs before a RakNetPacket is sent.
raknet.add_send_hook.purpose: Registers a callback that sees each outgoing network packet before it leaves the client. It operates below RemoteEvents, at the transport layer, which is where you look when the behaviour you care about is not exposed as a remote at all.
gotchas: Potassium-specific, and the lowest-level surface in the environment: you are handling raw network packets rather than Roblox objects.
Runs on the network path; slow callbacks cost you latency.
Malformed packets desync or disconnect the client rather than erroring cleanly.

raknet.remove_receive_hook.name: raknet.remove_receive_hook
raknet.remove_receive_hook.summary: Removes a previously registered receive hook.
raknet.remove_receive_hook.purpose: Unregisters a previously added receive hook.
gotchas: Potassium-specific, and the lowest-level surface in the environment: you are handling raw network packets rather than Roblox objects.

raknet.remove_send_hook.name: raknet.remove_send_hook
raknet.remove_send_hook.summary: Removes a previously registered send hook.
