raknet.remove_send_hook.purpose: Unregisters a previously added send hook. Leaving hooks installed after your script unloads keeps costing performance on every packet.
gotchas: Potassium-specific, and the lowest-level surface in the environment: you are handling raw network packets rather than Roblox objects.

raknet.send.name: raknet.send
raknet.send.summary: Sends a packet with a payload, priority, reliability and ordering channel.
raknet.send.purpose: Sends a packet directly, specifying payload, priority, reliability and ordering channel — the four parameters RakNet uses to decide how a message is delivered.
gotchas: Potassium-specific, and the lowest-level surface in the environment: you are handling raw network packets rather than Roblox objects.
Reliability and priority are enum values whose meaning comes from RakNet, not Roblox.

rconsoleclear.name: rconsoleclear
rconsoleclear.summary: Clears all text in the console.
rconsoleclear.purpose: Wipes the console contents while keeping the window open, for scripts that redraw a status view each tick.
gotchas: Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.

rconsolecreate.name: rconsolecreate
rconsolecreate.summary: Creates a console window. Only one console can be created.
rconsolecreate.purpose: Opens a native console window. Because it lives outside Roblox, game scripts cannot clear or read it, which makes it a reliable place to log while you work.
gotchas: Potassium-specific naming, widely implemented.
Only one console can exist at a time.
Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.

rconsoledestroy.name: rconsoledestroy
rconsoledestroy.summary: Destroys the console window. Text output to the console will be cleared.
rconsoledestroy.purpose: Closes the console window and discards its contents. Call it when your script unloads so you do not leave orphaned windows behind.
gotchas: Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.

rconsoleerror.name: rconsoleerror
rconsoleerror.summary: Prints a red message to the console, creating one if it does not exist.
rconsoleerror.purpose: Prints an error in red. Note that it prints; it does not raise a Luau error or stop execution.
gotchas: Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.
This is not `error`. Execution continues.

rconsoleinfo.name: rconsoleinfo
rconsoleinfo.summary: Prints a dark blue message to the console, creating one if it does not exist.
rconsoleinfo.purpose: Prints a message in the informational colour, so scanning a busy log for status lines is easier.
gotchas: Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.

rconsoleinput.name: rconsoleinput
rconsoleinput.summary: Receives input directly from the console. The calling thread is suspended until input is received.
rconsoleinput.purpose: Reads a line typed into the console, which gives a script a text input channel that does not require building any UI.
rconsoleinput.example:
rconsoleprint("enter a name: ")
local name = rconsoleinput()
print("hello", name)
gotchas: Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.
Suspends the calling thread until the user presses enter. Run it on its own thread.

rconsoleprint.name: rconsoleprint
rconsoleprint.summary: Prints to the console, creating one if it does not exist.
rconsoleprint.purpose: Writes plain text to the console, creating the window if it does not exist yet.
gotchas: Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.
No newline is added for you.

rconsolesettitle.name: rconsolesettitle
rconsolesettitle.summary: Sets the title of the console window.
rconsolesettitle.purpose: Sets the console window's title bar text, which is how you tell several script windows apart.
gotchas: Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.

rconsolewarn.name: rconsolewarn
rconsolewarn.summary: Prints a yellow message to the console, creating one if it does not exist.
rconsolewarn.purpose: Prints a warning in yellow, for conditions your script recovered from but you still want to see.
gotchas: Console output goes to a separate OS window, not the Roblox developer console.

readfile.name: readfile
readfile.summary: Reads the contents of a file at the specified path and returns it as a string.
readfile.purpose: Reads a file back as a string. Together with writefile it gives a script memory that survives rejoining the game.
readfile.example:
if isfile("myscript/config.json") then
    local config = game:GetService("HttpService"):JSONDecode(readfile("myscript/config.json"))
    print(config.walkSpeed)
end
gotchas: Errors if the file does not exist. Always guard with isfile.
Returns raw bytes for binary files, which will not survive being printed.

replicatesignal.name: replicatesignal
replicatesignal.summary: Replicates a signal to the server with the provided arguments, if the signal supports replication.
replicatesignal.purpose: The counterpart to firesignal for the small set of signals Roblox actually replicates to the server. Where firesignal is purely local, this makes the server observe the event, which is why the argument shape has to be exactly right.
replicatesignal.example:
-- Only works for signals on Roblox's replication whitelist
if cansignalreplicate(prompt.Triggered) then
    replicatesignal(prompt.Triggered)
end
gotchas: Fails outright if the signal is not replicable or the arguments do not match the expected types.
Check with cansignalreplicate first rather than wrapping in pcall and hoping.

request.name: request
request.summary: Sends an HTTP request using the provided configuration table. Yields until complete and returns a structured response.
request.purpose: A full HTTP client: methods, headers, cookies, bodies and a structured response. Roblox blocks outbound requests from game scripts, so this is how a script talks to an external API, fetches config, or reports back.
request.example:
local response = request({
    Url = "https://example.com/api",
    Method = "POST",
    Headers = { ["Content-Type"] = "application/json" },
    Body = game:GetService("HttpService"):JSONEncode({ id = 1 })
})

print(response.StatusCode, response.Success)
print(response.Body)
gotchas: Yields until the request completes. Do not call it inside a metamethod hook.
Executors add an identifying header of their own to every request; you are not anonymous to the endpoint.
Check StatusCode, not just Success.

restorefunction.name: restorefunction
restorefunction.summary: Restores a hooked function back to the original, even if it has been hooked multiple times.
restorefunction.purpose: Undoes hooking. Cleanly reverting a hook is harder than it looks, because a function may have been hooked several times by several scripts. restorefunction walks all the way back to the original implementation, which makes it the correct way to clean up before you unload a script.
restorefunction.example:
local original = hookfunction(target, myHook)
-- ... later, when your script unloads
restorefunction(target)
-- `target` now behaves exactly as it did before any hook
gotchas: Restores to the first original, not to the previous hook in the chain. If two scripts hooked the same function, restoring removes both.
Calling it on a function that was never hooked should be harmless, but not every executor guarantees that.

run_on_actor.name: run_on_actor
run_on_actor.summary: Executes a script on an actor.
run_on_actor.purpose: Executes your code inside an actor's context, which is the only way to touch state that lives in a parallel VM. Code running outside cannot see it at all.
run_on_actor.example:
local actor = getactors()[1]
run_on_actor(actor, [[
    print("running inside the actor")
]])
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Actors are Roblox's parallel Luau containers; behaviour here depends on the game actually using them.
The code is passed as a string, so it cannot capture your locals.
Each actor has its own environment; getgenv inside is not the same table as outside.

run_on_thread.name: run_on_thread
run_on_thread.summary: Executes a script on an actor thread.
run_on_thread.purpose: The finer-grained version of run_on_actor: run code on one specific actor thread rather than the actor as a whole.
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Actors are Roblox's parallel Luau containers; behaviour here depends on the game actually using them.

saveinstance.name: saveinstance
saveinstance.summary: Saves an instance in .rbxl or .rbxm format.
saveinstance.purpose: Serialises part of the game into an .rbxl or .rbxm file you can open in Studio. It is the standard way to study a game's structure and scripts offline instead of poking at it through a console.
gotchas: Potassium-specific in this exact form; option tables differ significantly between executors.
Large games take a long time and produce very large files.

setclipboard.name: setclipboard
setclipboard.summary: Sets text into the user's clipboard.
setclipboard.purpose: Writes text to the system clipboard, which is how tooling hands you output too long to read in a console — a dumped table, an asset ID, a decompiled script.
gotchas: Text only. Some implementations silently truncate very large strings.

setfflag.name: setfflag
setfflag.summary: Sets the value of a Fast Flag.
setfflag.purpose: Writes a Fast Flag at runtime, changing engine behaviour without editing client settings files.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Many flags are read once at startup, so setting them mid-session does nothing.
Values are passed as strings even for booleans and numbers.

setfpscap.name: setfpscap
setfpscap.summary: Sets the FPS cap for the client.
setfpscap.purpose: Changes the client's frame rate limit. Raising it is the common use; lowering it is a legitimate way to reduce load while a script runs in the background.
setfpscap.example:
setfpscap(240)
setfpscap(0)   -- 0 means uncapped on most implementations
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Physics behaviour in some games is frame-rate dependent, so a very high cap changes gameplay.

sethiddenproperty.name: sethiddenproperty
sethiddenproperty.signature: function sethiddenproperty(instance: Instance, property_name: string, property_value: any): boolean
sethiddenproperty.summary: Assigns a value to a hidden or non-scriptable property of an Instance, even if that property is normally read-only or inaccessible.
sethiddenproperty.purpose: Writes to a property normal Luau refuses to write, including ones that are read-only from a script's perspective. It is the write half of hidden-property access.
gotchas: Many hidden properties are client-side only; the server keeps its own value and ignores yours.
Writing a wrong type can crash the client rather than error.

setnamecallmethod.name: setnamecallmethod
setnamecallmethod.purpose: Rewrites which method the current __namecall invocation will resolve to, letting a hook redirect a call to a different method instead of blocking or faking its return value.
setnamecallmethod.example:
local old
old = hookmetamethod(game, "__namecall", function(self, ...)
    if getnamecallmethod() == "Kick" then
        setnamecallmethod("GetFullName")  -- turn a kick into something harmless
    end
    return old(self, ...)
end)
gotchas: Potassium-specific; not part of the sUNC standard.
The replacement method must accept the arguments already on the stack, or the call errors.

setproximitypromptduration.name: setproximitypromptduration
setproximitypromptduration.summary: Sets the value of a proximity prompt's duration.
setproximitypromptduration.purpose: Sets how long a prompt must be held. Setting it to zero turns every hold prompt into an instant one without firing anything, which is quieter than calling fireproximityprompt repeatedly.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Client-side only; a server that times interactions still sees the real elapsed time.

setrawmetatable.name: setrawmetatable
setrawmetatable.signature: function setrawmetatable<T>(object: T & ({ any } | userdata), metatable: { any }): T
setrawmetatable.summary: Forcibly sets the metatable of a value, bypassing the __metatable protection field.
setrawmetatable.purpose: Assigns a metatable to a value even when a __metatable field would normally block it. Where getrawmetatable lets you read the locked table, this lets you replace it wholesale, which is the heavier option when hooking individual metamethods is not enough.
gotchas: Replacing a shared metatable rather than editing it breaks every object that uses it.
Returns the object, so you can chain, but the mutation happens in place.

setrbxclipboard.name: setrbxclipboard
setrbxclipboard.summary: Sets data into the Roblox Studio clipboard.
setrbxclipboard.purpose: Puts instance data into the Roblox Studio clipboard, so you can paste real objects straight into Studio rather than saving a file first.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Requires Studio to be running to be of any use.

setreadonly.name: setreadonly
setreadonly.summary: Sets whether a table is readonly or writable.
setreadonly.purpose: Luau marks core tables readonly so game code cannot patch them. This flips that flag, and it is the step people forget: reading a locked metatable works, writing to it does not, until you unlock it.
setreadonly.example:
local mt = getrawmetatable(game)
print(isreadonly(mt))     -- true
setreadonly(mt, false)    -- unlock
mt.__namecall = myHook
setreadonly(mt, true)     -- lock again, leave no trace
gotchas: Leaving a core table writable is detectable. Re-lock immediately after editing.
Readonly is a property of the table, not of your access to it, so unlocking affects the whole game.

setrenderproperty.name: setrenderproperty
setrenderproperty.signature: function setrenderproperty(drawing: Drawing, property: string, value: any): ()
setrenderproperty.summary: Assigns a value to a property of a Drawing object. Behaves identically to object[property] = value, but is useful for dynamic or abstracted property access.
setrenderproperty.purpose: Writes a drawing property by name, the companion to getrenderproperty for property-table-driven UI code.
setrenderproperty.example:
for name, value in pairs({ Visible = true, Thickness = 3 }) do
    setrenderproperty(box, name, value)
end
gotchas: An invalid property name errors on some implementations and is silently ignored on others.

setscriptable.name: setscriptable
setscriptable.signature: function setscriptable(instance: Instance, property_name: string, state: boolean): boolean | nil
setscriptable.summary: Toggles the scriptability of a hidden or non-scriptable property. When made scriptable, it can be read or assigned through standard indexing.
setscriptable.purpose: Flips a property's scriptable flag, so a hidden property becomes readable and writable with normal dot syntax for as long as the flag is set. Convenient when you need to touch the same property repeatedly.
setscriptable.example:
local previous = setscriptable(workspace.Part, "MeshId", true)
workspace.Part.MeshId = "rbxassetid://0"
setscriptable(workspace.Part, "MeshId", previous)  -- restore
gotchas: Returns the previous state, which you should restore. Leaving properties scriptable is a visible change to the environment.
The flag applies to the class, not just your instance, on some implementations.

setsimulationradius.name: setsimulationradius
setsimulationradius.summary: Sets the simulation radius of the LocalPlayer.
setsimulationradius.purpose: Requests a larger physics-simulation radius, which historically extended network ownership to distant parts and let a client move things far away.
gotchas: Potassium-specific.
Widely detected and largely mitigated server-side on modern Roblox. Treat it as unreliable rather than a guarantee.

setstackhidden.name: setstackhidden
setstackhidden.summary: Hide a function from call-stack based detections.
setstackhidden.purpose: Removes a function from the visible call stack, so that stack inspection performed further down the call chain does not reveal that your code is in it. It exists because call-stack inspection is a common way for game code to tell who called it.
setstackhidden.example:
local function myHook(...)
    return original(...)
end

setstackhidden(myHook, true)  -- omit this frame from stack walks
gotchas: Potassium-specific. Nothing equivalent is part of the sUNC standard.
Hiding a frame does not hide side effects, timing, or the fact that a function was replaced.

setthreadidentity.name: setthreadidentity
setthreadidentity.summary: Sets the current Luau thread identity and the capabilities matching that identity.
setthreadidentity.purpose: Changes the current thread's identity and the capabilities that come with it. Raising it unlocks protected APIs; lowering it is how you make your calls look like ordinary game code to anything that inspects identity.
gotchas: Forgetting to restore leaves later code running at the wrong level and produces confusing permission errors.
Identity affects the thread, so a yield inside the changed section can hand the wrong identity to resumed code.
Setting an identity you do not actually have capabilities for is one of the things sUNC tests behaviourally.

writefile.name: writefile
writefile.summary: Writes data to a file at the specified path, overwriting existing contents.
writefile.purpose: Writes a file into the executor's sandboxed workspace folder. This is how scripts persist configuration, cache downloaded assets, and dump data for you to read outside the game.
gotchas: Overwrites without warning. Use appendfile to add to a file.
Parent folders are not created automatically; call makefolder first.
Paths are relative to the executor's workspace directory. Absolute paths and .. traversal are blocked.

concepts.title: What sUNC and Potassium actually are
concepts.lede: Two documents that describe the same environment from different angles: one is a standard, the other is an implementation.
concepts.body:
Roblox gives a LocalScript a deliberately small world. No filesystem, no HTTP, no loadstring, no way to read another script's variables. An executor is a program that runs Luau code inside the Roblox client with those limits removed, and the functions it adds are what this site documents.

The problem is that every executor added them independently. The same idea appeared under three names, with three signatures and three sets of edge cases, and a script written for one silently broke on another.

**UNC** (Unified Naming Convention) was the first attempt to fix that: a shared list of names and signatures so a script could assume `getgenv` meant the same thing everywhere. It worked until it did not. UNC checked that a function *existed*, not that it *worked*, so an executor could score highly by defining a hundred functions that returned nil.

**sUNC** (senS' Unified Naming Convention) is the successor built around that failure. It tests behaviour: it calls the function, checks the return type, checks the edge cases, and checks that the implementation is not simply pretending. Its own summary of the difference is that you should not spoof it, you should prove it. Results are cryptographically signed so a published score cannot be edited afterwards, and the test only runs inside the official sUNC game so the environment cannot be faked around it.

**Potassium** is an executor, not a standard. Its documentation describes what its own environment provides, which follows UNC with, in its words, a lot of tweaks and additions. It implements essentially all of the sUNC surface and then adds large areas sUNC does not cover at all: actors, RakNet packet hooks, off-thread hooking, a regex library, immediate-mode drawing.

That relationship is why every entry on this site carries an availability tag. **In both** means the function is part of the tested standard and Potassium implements it, so a script using it is portable. **Potassium only** means it works today, in that executor, and a script relying on it will not run elsewhere. **sUNC only** is rare, and currently means `checkcaller` and `clonefunction`: tested by the standard but not documented in Potassium's reference under those names.

Portability is the practical reason to care. Availability is not a quality ranking.

concepts.title: C closures and Lua closures
concepts.lede: Two kinds of function live in the same environment, and almost every hooking bug comes from confusing them.
concepts.body:
A **Lua closure** is a function compiled from Luau source. It has bytecode, a constant table, a list of upvalues, and nested prototypes. Everything in the debug library that reads a function reads this kind.

A **C closure** is a function implemented in C: `print`, `game.GetService`, and every native the engine or your executor provides. It has no bytecode to read, no constants, no protos. Calling `debug.getconstants` on one fails.

You can always tell them apart with `iscclosure` and `islclosure`, and for a valid function exactly one of them is true.

This distinction has three practical consequences.

**Hooking rules differ.** Replacing a C function with a plain Lua function is a type mismatch that many executors reject, and even where it is allowed, the difference is visible to anything that checks. `newcclosure` exists to wrap a Lua function so it reports as a C closure.

**Introspection only works one way.** If you want to read what a function does — its constants, its upvalues, its inner functions — it has to be a Lua closure. Checking with `islclosure` first turns a confusing error into a clean branch.

**Identity is separate from behaviour.** `clonefunction` gives you a function that does the same thing but is a different object, so hooking one leaves the other untouched. This is how you keep a private copy of `print` that survives someone else hooking the global one.

`isexecutorclosure` cuts across both categories: it asks who created the function rather than what kind it is. Anything from `loadstring`, `getscriptclosure`, or your own script is an executor closure, and sUNC checks all three cases rather than just the obvious one.

concepts.title: Metatables, __index and __namecall
concepts.lede: Why hooking one table changes the behaviour of the entire game.
concepts.body:
Every Roblox instance is a userdata whose behaviour comes from a shared metatable. When you write `part.Size`, Luau does not look up a field: it calls `__index` on that metatable. When you write `part:Destroy()`, it calls `__namecall`. The same two functions handle every property read and every method call in the game.

That is what makes them worth hooking. You do not have to find the function a game uses to fire a remote; you hook `__namecall` once and see all of them.

Getting there takes three steps, and each has a trap.

**Reading the metatable.** `getmetatable(game)` returns a string, because Roblox sets `__metatable` to lock it. `getrawmetatable` ignores the lock and returns the real table.

**Unlocking it.** The metatable is readonly. Assigning to it errors until you call `setreadonly(mt, false)`, and leaving it unlocked afterwards is itself a detectable change — lock it again when you are done. `hookmetamethod` handles this for you, which is a good reason to prefer it over editing the table by hand.

**Knowing which method fired.** `__namecall` receives the object and the arguments but not the method name. `getnamecallmethod` supplies it. Without that call, a `__namecall` hook cannot tell `FireServer` from `GetChildren`.

Two rules keep `__namecall` hooks from breaking games. Do not yield inside one: you are running on the game's thread, and yielding there stalls the caller. And guard with `checkcaller`, because your hook fires for your own calls too, and a hook that intercepts itself produces failures that look nothing like their cause.

One more thing worth internalising: the metatable is shared. There is one metatable behind every instance in the game. A change is never scoped to the object you passed in.

concepts.title: getgenv, getrenv, getsenv, gettenv
concepts.lede: Four global tables, four different scopes, and picking the wrong one is the most common beginner mistake in the whole environment.
concepts.body:
Luau code always runs against some table of globals. The executor environment exposes four of them, and they are not interchangeable.

**getgenv** is yours. It is shared between every script your executor runs, and nothing else. This is where a script puts a load guard so re-executing does not start a second copy of every loop, and where two of your scripts agree on a configuration table. Because it is shared with every other script the user runs, use a distinctive key: `getgenv().Config` will collide with somebody.

**getrenv** is the game's. It is the environment Roblox's own scripts see. Reading it shows you the globals the game defined; writing to it changes what the game sees, which is powerful and extremely visible. Note that `getrenv().print` and your `print` are different objects, so hooking one does nothing to the other — a subtlety that costs people hours.

**getsenv** is one specific script's. Given a running script, you get its globals, which usually includes the functions it defined. This is how you call a game function that was never exposed anywhere. It only works while the script is running, and returns nil otherwise.

**gettenv** is one thread's. Threads can carry their own environment, and this reads it — useful when you have pulled a thread out of the registry or an actor and have no script to go with it.

Two related tables sit underneath all of this. `getreg` returns the Luau registry, where the C side keeps strong references to threads and callbacks that no Lua variable points at. `getgc` returns what the garbage collector is tracking. Neither is an environment, but both are where you look when a value has no reachable name.

If a hook on a global does not fire, the cause is often `safeenv`, a Luau optimisation that lets the VM skip metatable lookups on globals it believes are untouched. `debug.getsafeenv` reads that flag and `debug.setsafeenv` clears it.

concepts.title: Constants, upvalues and protos
concepts.lede: The three things a compiled Luau function carries, and what each one lets you change.
concepts.body:
Roblox ships bytecode to the client, never source. A compiled function is not a black box though: it carries three readable structures, and the debug library exposes all three.

**Constants** are the literals baked into the code — the number 100, the string "FireServer", the names of globals it calls. `debug.getconstants` lists them. They tell you what a function references, which is how you identify the right function among dozens with similar shapes. `debug.setconstant` rewrites one, which patches behaviour without replacing the function.

**Upvalues** are the variables the function captured from its enclosing scope: live state, not literals. `debug.getupvalues` reads them, `debug.setupvalue` writes them. The distinction from constants matters — a value that changes while the game runs is an upvalue, and setting a constant will not touch it.

**Protos** are the compiled templates of functions defined inside the function. `debug.getprotos` lists them, which is how you reach an anonymous callback that was never assigned to anything you can see. There is a catch: a proto is a template with empty upvalues, so calling it usually errors. `debug.getproto(fn, index, true)` returns the live closures created from that template instead, with real state attached. That third argument is the difference between a useless clone and the actual running function.

Two rules apply to all of this. It works on Lua closures only, so check `islclosure` first. And indices are not stable across game updates: match on values, never on positions, or your script breaks the next time the developer adds a line.

Above the function level, `debug.getstack` reads the values in a live stack frame and `debug.setstack` writes them, which is the most surgical patch available and the most fragile.

concepts.title: Thread identity and who is calling
concepts.lede: The same line of code can succeed or throw depending on which thread runs it.
concepts.body:
Roblox attaches an identity level to every thread, and that identity decides what the code on it may do: which services it can reach, which properties it can write, whether protected APIs are available. An executor thread normally runs at a high identity, which is why your code can do things a LocalScript cannot.

`getthreadidentity` reads the current level and `setthreadidentity` changes it. Lowering it deliberately is a real technique — running a call at the identity a normal game script would have makes the call behave the way the game expects. Always restore the previous value, because identity belongs to the thread and any code that runs after you on that thread inherits whatever you left behind.

Separately from identity, hooks need to answer a question constantly: was this call mine or the game's?

**checkcaller** answers for the running thread. Inside a hook it returns true when your own code triggered the call, which is how a hook passes your calls through untouched instead of intercepting itself. A hook without this eventually recurses into its own logic and produces a bug that looks like anything except its actual cause.

**getcallingscript** answers with more precision: which script triggered execution. That lets a hook treat one script differently from another rather than applying a blanket rule.

**isourthread** asks about a thread you are holding rather than the one you are on, which is what you need when filtering a list of threads from the registry or from actors.

**debug.getcallstack** gives you the whole chain at once, and `setstackhidden` removes a frame from it.

Yielding interacts with all of this. If you change identity, yield, and let something else resume on that thread, the identity you set is still in effect for code that never asked for it.

concepts.title: Finding things with the garbage collector
concepts.lede: When there is no reference to the thing you want, you search the heap for it.
concepts.body:
Most of what a game keeps is unreachable from outside. A module returns a table into a local variable, a connection captures a closure, and nothing you can index leads to either of them. The garbage collector, however, is tracking all of it, because it has to know what is still alive.

`getgc` returns that list: every live function and userdata, plus every table if you pass `true`. Forgetting that argument is the reason people spend an afternoon wondering why their table is not in there.

Scanning it yourself works and is slow. `filtergc` does the same search natively — describe the shape you want, a function with a given name, a table with certain keys, and the executor matches it in C. It is faster by a wide margin and much less code. The `IgnoreExecutor` option matters more than it looks: without it, your own closures match your own filters.

Two habits make GC searching survivable. Store what you find immediately, since an object can be collected between the scan and the use. And never scan in a loop — a full GC walk every frame will stutter the game visibly, which is both a performance problem and a behavioural signal.

The registry, via `getreg` or `debug.getregistry`, is the other half of this. It holds strong references the C side needs, so anything in it is guaranteed alive: engine callbacks, threads, userdata shared across the boundary. Read it freely; writing to it creates a reference that is never collected.

concepts.title: The instance cache and reference identity
concepts.lede: Two references can point at the same object and still not be equal, and games check exactly that.
concepts.body:
Roblox keeps a cache mapping engine objects to the userdata your Luau code holds. Ask for `game.Players.LocalPlayer` twice and you get the same object both times, which is why `==` normally works the way you expect.

That predictability is also a detection surface. If the reference you are using is the same object the game is using, anything you do through it is attributable to whoever holds that reference.

`cloneref` breaks the link. It returns a second reference to the same underlying instance which is not equal to the original. The game keeps its reference, you have yours, and comparisons between them fail.

That failure is the cost. Once clonerefs are circulating, `==` stops answering the question you meant, so `compareinstances` exists to compare the underlying objects properly. Any of your code that compared instances with `==` needs revisiting.

Potassium exposes the cache directly. `cache.iscached` asks whether an instance is in it, `cache.invalidate` removes an entry so the next lookup produces a fresh object, and `cache.replace` makes a lookup return a different instance entirely. Where `cloneref` changes what you hold, `cache.replace` changes what the game gets.

None of this hides what you do to an object. It changes who appears to be doing it.

concepts.title: Hooking, cleanly
concepts.lede: Replacing a function is easy. Replacing it without breaking the game, or yourself, is the actual skill.
concepts.body:
`hookfunction` swaps a function's implementation and hands you the original. That single sentence hides most of the difficulty.

**Call the original you were given, not the name you hooked.** Calling the name calls your hook, which calls the name, which calls your hook. The stack overflow that follows is the first hooking bug everyone writes.

**Match the closure type.** Hooking a C function with a plain Lua closure is rejected or detectable depending on the executor. Wrap your hook in `newcclosure` when the target is a C closure, and keep the wrapped function around rather than wrapping on every call.

**Keep hooks small.** Upvalue-count limits apply on some implementations, so hook a thin wrapper that calls your real logic instead of hooking a large closure directly.

**Guard with checkcaller.** Your hook fires for your own calls too. Passing your own calls straight through avoids a whole class of confusing failures.

**Never yield in a metamethod hook.** `__index` and `__namecall` run on the game's thread. Yielding there stalls the caller, and the symptom appears somewhere unrelated.

**Clean up.** `restorefunction` walks a function back to its original implementation, which matters because it may have been hooked more than once. `isfunctionhooked` lets you avoid double-hooking on a re-execute. A script that hooks on every run without checking will chain hooks onto its own previous hooks until something breaks.

For metamethods specifically, prefer `hookmetamethod` over editing the raw metatable. It handles the unlock-and-relock cycle, and leaving a core metatable writable is a state change anything can notice.

Potassium adds `oth.hook`, which runs the hook body on an isolated thread rather than the caller's. It is aimed at C functions where an ordinary hook is more constrained. The trade-off is that your hook is no longer on the caller's thread, so `checkcaller` and thread identity read differently inside it, and you retrieve the original through `oth.get_root_callback` instead of a saved reference.

concepts.title: Signals: firing, replicating, and what the server sees
concepts.lede: firesignal does not talk to the server. That one fact resolves most confusion in this library.
concepts.body:
An `RBXScriptSignal` normally hides its listeners. `getconnections` returns them as connection objects, each exposing the listener function plus `Disable`, `Enable` and `Fire`. Disabling one listener is far more precise than replacing the function it points at, and `Disable` is reversible where `Disconnect` is not.

`firesignal` invokes every Lua listener on a signal with arguments you choose. It runs entirely on your client. The game's client-side code reacts as though the event happened; the server learns nothing. Scripts that appear to work locally and change nothing on the server are almost always built on this misunderstanding.

`replicatesignal` is the narrow exception. Roblox permits clients to replicate a specific whitelisted set of signals, and for those, the server genuinely observes the event. Because the server validates it, the arguments have to be exactly right, which is what the surrounding functions are for: `cansignalreplicate` tells you whether a signal qualifies, `getsignalarguments` and `getsignalargumentsinfo` tell you what to pass, and `getsignalwhitelist` lists everything eligible.

The general shape to remember: local effects are cheap and easy, server-visible effects are constrained by what Roblox already allows. No function in this library changes that boundary.
